The reading room

Sources reflect their publishers’ perspectives and dates. A government directory describes an administrative system; a community account has a different purpose.

Outside archives can contain outdated terminology. The annotations and profile notes provide a starting point for reading critically.

Sources

Download: Source catalogue (JSON) · Data & field guide. Access and inspection limits are recorded per profile; linked works retain their own terms.

Government / historical primary legal document1936 Government Printing Office text transcribed by University of Oklahoma Native American Constitution and Law Digitization ProjectSource 1

Constitution and Bylaws of the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation, approved April20,1936 ↗

Historical governing instrument identifying the joint Tribes, territorial jurisdiction, council powers, land provisions and amendment process. Its adoption certification dates the vote to March21,1936 and approval to April20. The transcription contains apparent errors; do not silently correct its text or present 1936 provisions as verified current law.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete HTML transcription including constitution articlesI–X, bylawsI–VI and adoption/approval certification, lines53–266. Original scan and amendments not inspected.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Ishak Indigenous People ↗

Publication: 2022-08-15 (updated 2024-02-19)

Bethke, Brandi, Sarah Trabert, and Gary McAdams. 2024. “Anchoring Sovereignty in Space: Documenting Places of Wichita Community Building in the Twentieth Century.” American Antiquity 89(3): 360–377. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2024.23.

Publication: 2024-05-13

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public full HTML, publisher-labelled Open Access

Access note: The complete article HTML was available without login. Primary metadata supplies authors, affiliations, DOI, issue/pages, publication date and CC BY4.0 license. Gary McAdams is explicitly affiliated with Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; no other author's ancestry is inferred. The methods state Tribal Executive Committee involvement and participant consent, and distinguish academic interpretation from community memories. Raw interviews, field notes and spatial datasets are held by named offices and may be accessible only at their discretion; none were requested or accessed. No ceremonial descriptions, stories, archaeological location codes, coordinates, photographs or maps are proposed for reproduction.

Lipan Apache Placenames of Augustina Zuazua: Some Structural and Discursive Features ↗

Publication: June 2007

A linguistic and ethnohistorical analysis centered on Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative to Harry Hoijer. Webster examines how place names work in that account and cautions that a small sample from one narrator cannot support broad claims about all Lipan Apache naming practices. The article’s abstract and main text refer to 22 names, while a note identifies a twenty-third; several locations remain unidentified. These names are not a surveyed boundary or a statement of present-day territorial extent.

Historia de la tribu kikapú y de su problemática ↗

Publication: 2010; chapter pages 101–113

This 2010 Spanish-language book chapter surveys Kickapoo histories from the Great Lakes to Coahuila and Texas and discusses the formation of the Texas community, cross-border relations, land, federal recognition, and the Lucky Eagle casino context. It is a scholarly synthesis by one author drawing on earlier publications and field interviews with Kickapoo and Múzquiz residents (1996–2002); its interpretations are not a community-authored consensus. The chapter itself notes contradictory dates and figures in cited works, including the 1873 El Remolino attack and land-area totals. Read those passages as attributed historical claims rather than settled facts. The repository lists open access and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; only a link is reproduced here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full 13-page chapter read (printed pages 101–113), including historical narrative, El Nacimiento and Texas sections, source notes, and references.

Ethnic Consciousness in Cultural Survival: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians and the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas ↗

Publication: 2017

This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. Mager identifies documentary research, participant observation, and interviews as methods and cites interviews conducted from 1995 to 2015, along with the Texas Tribe’s 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. Selected passages discuss land acquisition and economic history; the author’s theory of “ethnic consciousness,” causal claims, and generalizations remain her interpretation, not a community consensus. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read article metadata and research-method statement (printed pp.47–48), Kickapoo-focused land and Texas economic-history passages (printed pp.61–63), and the corresponding cited notes on printed p.71. The comparative sections about Morongo and detailed ceremonial/cultural descriptions were not used. Claims are attributed to the author and the dates/interview sources stated in her notes.

Historical primary account / archival publicationGeorge A. Root, editor; Kansas Historical Society; account recorded by Franklin G. AdamsSource 545

No-ko-aht’s Talk: A Kickapoo Chief’s Account of a Tribal Journey from Kansas to Mexico and Return in the Sixties ↗

Publication: Interview recorded May 31, 1867; edited/published February 1932, Kansas Historical Quarterly 1(2), pp. 153–159

The article prints a May 31, 1867 account attributed to Kickapoo leader No-ko-aht and recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams. No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full transcribed article and footnotes read, pp.153–159. Inspected the editor’s account and the attributed No-ko-aht statement; no independent corroboration of every event, date, casualty number, or quotation was established.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Access note: Public transcription hosted by Kansas Historical Society; source page states digitized with permission. Historical spellings, editorial framing, and one illegible passage are retained as source limitations.

Tribal news release / contemporary land stewardshipGrand Portage Band of Lake Superior ChippewaSource 570

Grand Portage Band Regains Historic Tribal Land ↗

Publication: March 16, 2026

A Grand Portage Band news release reports that a February 2026 acquisition restored three parcels totaling about 87 acres to Band ownership through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. The Band describes three distinct routes by which those parcels left Band ownership: 1854 treaty cession, state school-trust transfer, and allotment. This is a direct community source for the Bands current action and its historical interpretation; the underlying treaty, land-title chain, tax records, and allotment documents were not independently checked. The Bands broad discussion of allotment policy remains attributed to the release and is not generalized to every Ojibwe Band. A linked map/images package is not included.

Letter from J. W. Throckmorton to the U.S. Commissioner of Indian Affairs, September 20, 1866 ↗

Publication: September 20, 1866 (document); edited volume publication date not established in this review

A contemporary state-executive letter asking federal officials to provide Tonkawa survivors with food, land, an agent and other assistance after their return to Texas. Throckmorton gives one official explanation for the attack and presents the survivors’ needs alongside frontier-security concerns. The language, reported figures and causal account are the governor’s claims, not a Tonkawa voice, a neutral count, or proof that the requests were implemented.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full transcribed letter read across printed pp. 110–112 in the edited volume. The archive page OCR and displayed text were inspected; the original Executive Record Book manuscript, federal response and any later appropriation or land transfer were not checked. The unrelated next letter beginning on p. 112 was excluded.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Supporting catalogue record for the multination 1846 treaty, including related National Archives file units and the March 8, 1847 ratification date. Profile-specific review notes (2)

One linked work can have different uses and inspection limits in different profiles. A supporting or identity check is not a substantive history review.

Lipan Apache

Recorded perspective/type: Archive / government catalogue

Supporting catalogue record for the multination 1846 treaty, including related National Archives file units and the March 8, 1847 ratification date. Its “Named Native nations” indexing does not list Lipan even though the catalogue title and treaty text do; this is recorded as a catalogue scope/indexing issue, not an inference about the treaty parties. Excluded from the substantive-work count because the treaty itself is counted once.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

Tonkawa

Recorded perspective/type: Primary treaty text and archival record

The National Archives / Indigenous Digital Archive record supplies the treaty title, a scan viewer with transcribed text, and links to separate Senate and presidential ratification records. The treaty preamble and signatory pages name the Tonkawa as “Long-wha” / “Tonkaways” among multiple Native parties. Its articles record the U.S. government’s terms on trade, prisoners, criminal complaints, and proposed services. This is a federal treaty text in its own period language, not a Tonkawa-authored interpretation or proof of implementation. The archive’s normalized named-nation fields omit Tonkawa despite the title and treaty pages; that indexing discrepancy is retained.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete visible metadata and the scan viewer’s transcribed/OCR text for viewer pages 2–10: treaty preamble and articles (pages 2–7) plus signatory lists, including the Tonkawa/Tonkaways page (page 10). The 22-page archival object’s linked Senate advice-and-consent and presidential ratification instruments, other duplicate copies, and later implementation records were not inspected. No signatory marks were individually identified or interpreted.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Historical Sketches of the Several Indian Tribes in Louisiana: Adaize account ↗

Publication: 1808

1805 account, communicated with Jefferson's 1806 message; inspected in a dated 1808 Boston reprint, printed pp. 42–44, especially the complete Adaize entry on p. 44 (PDF p. 52). Legal primary source / court opinionJustia, reproducing a reported federal district-court opinionSource 762

Leech Lake Band of Chippewa Indians v. Herbst, 334 F. Supp. 1001 (D. Minn. 1971) ↗

Publication: December 10, 1971

The complete reported opinion addresses whether Leech Lake Band members could fish, hunt, and gather wild rice on public lands and waters within the Leech Lake Reservation free from Minnesota game and fish laws. The court held that treaty rights had not been abrogated by the Nelson Act and declared those activities protected on the specified public lands and waters. The opinion did not accept the Band’s claim to exclusive regulatory authority over all fishing, hunting, and ricing. This is a dated judicial holding in a particular case, not a statement of current regulations or a substitute for later law.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the full opinion and notes (reported text at pages 1001–1010; Justia lines 38–143). The opinion recounts the litigants’ positions, testimony, treaty/legal analysis, and the court’s narrow declaratory judgment. The 1855/1864/1867 treaty originals, trial exhibits, and later proceedings were not independently inspected in this entry.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

State v. Forge, 262 N.W.2d 341 (Minn. 1977) ↗

Publication: October 14, 1977

The full opinion recounts the Leech Lake Band’s 1969 federal lawsuit, the 1971 Herbst decision, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, and challenges to Minnesota’s reservation fishing stamp. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that Minnesota Chippewa Tribe members retained treaty rights and upheld the 1973 statutory compromise and the convictions of nonmembers who fished without the stamp. This later ruling supplies important historical context for the 1971 opinion; it does not establish every present-day regulation or decide all treaty-right questions.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the full reported opinion and notes (262 N.W.2d 341–349; Justia lines 38–163), including its description of the 1971 federal case, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, statutory terms, holding, and express limits on what issues the appeal decided. The settlement document, current statute and later court cases were not separately reviewed.

Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. Cummins et al., Document 48 (D. Minn. Feb. 24, 2023) ↗

Publication: February 24, 2023

In a challenge to a Forest Service land exchange for the proposed NorthMet mine, the District Court denied PolyMet’s motion to dismiss. At this pleading-stage ruling, it accepted the complaint’s allegation that the exchange could remove access to 6,650 acres used for the Band’s treaty rights and held that the Band had standing to assert its own 1854 Treaty usufructuary interests; those rights were not exclusively individual member rights. This is not a decision on the merits of the land exchange or the ultimate project outcome. The alleged access loss is described as a complaint allegation, not a factual finding.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the full 18-page opinion as reproduced on Justia, including the docket/date and disposition (lines 38–50), the complaint’s background and stated alleged injury (lines 51–63), the treaty and tribal-right analysis (lines 64–98), and the order denying dismissal (lines 103–110). The complaint and docket exhibits, Forest Service Record of Decision, environmental review, and later case history were not independently inspected.

Constitution of the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas, with scanned amendment and federal election/approval records ↗

Publication: 1989 constitution; amendment/election papers 2017 and 2018

The Tribe-hosted 20-page scan includes the constitution and BIA election/approval papers from 1989, 2017, and 2018. The preamble describes organization as a Tribe separate and apart from the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; the 1989 approval certificate states that its approval does not authorize action contrary to federal law. Later papers document amendments to constitutional provisions. The scan’s cover wording and included amendment-number labels are not fully consistent, and it is not independently verified here as the currently operative consolidated constitution. It is a primary historical/governance record, not legal advice or a source for private enrollment details.

Materials Related to the Co-Management of the Chippewa National Forest: The Right to Self-Governance — Historical and Current Overview of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe ↗

Publication: Undated compilation; contains a 2019 Memorandum of Understanding and a 2020 briefing presentation

A first-party Leech Lake Band educational and resource-management account, created to explain historical events, treaties, the Band’s government, and its agency relationships to Band staff and citizens. The historical overview narrates the 1837, 1854, 1855, 1864, and 1867 treaty sequence, later allotment and logging, the 1898 Sugar Point conflict, and the Band’s resource-governance work. Treaty-right and legal conclusions are presented as the Band’s institutional interpretation; the underlying treaty instruments, court opinions, and cited historical records were not independently checked in this source review. The booklet also includes later co-management materials that should be read as dated documents, not assumed to describe every current policy.

It is not used as a complete statement of current ordinances or present policy; current legal amendments were not checked, and period-specific membership wording is not repeated in this profile.

Peer-reviewed community-based participatory researchPublic Health Reviews 38 (2017), article 30; University of New Mexico and Mescalero Apache community partnership; PubMed Central open-access copySource 1332

The piloting of a culturally centered American Indian family prevention program: a CBPR partnership between Mescalero Apache and the University of New Mexico ↗

Publication: December 22, 2017

A peer-reviewed article coauthored by University of New Mexico researchers and staff affiliated with the Mescalero Apache Prevention Program and System of Care. It reports that the Tribe requested the partnership, that a Tribal Council resolution supported co-writing and co-submission, and that a Mescalero Apache Tribal Research Team adapted and piloted a family program. The authors state the manuscript received Tribal Council and Southwest Tribal IRB approval. The study concerns a specific 2013–2014 pilot, not current program availability, all Mescalero families, or long-term outcomes. Its brief historical statements—including a broad homeland context spanning parts of Texas, Arizona and Mexico—remain attributed to the article; the underlying historical records were not checked here. The Atlas does not reproduce curriculum materials, participant data, images, or private content.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the open-access article body: publication metadata, abstract, research-partnership and historical-background sections, team formation and curriculum adaptation, pilot design and sample, selected results, discussion/conclusion, acknowledgments, approval statement and data-availability note (visible sections around lines 33–160, 176–215, 224–300 and 373). The pilot is discussed only as a dated collaborative research project; small sample, incomplete follow-up, short duration, and the authors’ statement that no difference in substance use was observed are kept in view. No participant-level data, session materials, images or follow-up study results were accessed. Cited historical works were not independently reviewed.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5785102/

Primary legal decisionSupreme Court of the United StatesSource 1625

Idaho v. United States, 533 U.S. 262 ↗

Publication: 2001

Read the opinion in volume 533, pp. 262–280 (bound PDF pp. 265–280 in an 868-page volume). The Court held that the United States holds in trust for the Tribe the specified submerged lands within the reservation, including portions of the lake and river. The holding is limited to title in the disputed submerged lands; it is not a ruling that the Tribe owns the whole lake or every basin interest.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

This is a Republic of Texas diplomatic document in colonial/state language, mediated through a later edited transcription. Its text does not establish that the proposed agreement was ratified, implemented, or accepted as a lasting boundary by the named peoples. It is not a present homeland map.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Transcript of the February 23, 1836 document on printed pages 14–15 of volume I reviewed through the Texas History Trust/University of North Texas text. The treaty’s opening and land-boundary article were inspected; the full volume, manuscript original, signatures and implementation record were not reviewed.

Primary community petition and member testimony in a congressional recordTonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial SetSource 1755

Memorial of the Tonkawa Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma relating to claims against the United States — S. Doc. 60-206 ↗

Publication: Memorial adopted January 2, 1907; presented to Senate January 28, 1908

This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. The memorial’s account should be read alongside the 1892 federal document, which records commissioners’ contrasting assessment. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. No individualized allotment or burial site details were published.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Tonkawa Indians at Fort Griffin, Texas — H. Ex. Doc. 44-102 ↗

Publication: February 1, 1876; compiles correspondence from 1872–1876

The congressional document records federal officials’ accounts of a small Lipan group moving from Fort Sill to Fort Griffin in 1874, subsequent ration decisions affecting Tonkawa and Lipan people there, and proposed removal options. The 1875 Interior Department letter reports kinship through intermarriage and discusses a possible consolidation; it is an official’s account and recommendation, not a Lipan-authored history or evidence that the proposal was implemented. It must not be generalized to all Lipan people or treated as proof of incorporation into Mescalero Apache.

Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Richards, No. 94-50369 (corrected opinion following rehearing) ↗

Publication: Corrected opinion filed February 9, 1996; substituted after rehearing for the October 23, 1995 opinion

The corrected February 9, 1996 appellate opinion recounts the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s suit over the 1866 Texas act, which provided for a one-league home site selected by the Governor. The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Texas and held that the act did not create a perfected, self-executing grant under the record and statutory language before the panel. The decision addresses that statute and case; it is not a general historical-homeland survey, a statement about present Tonkawa identity, or current legal advice. The court states that the opinion replaced its October 1995 version after rehearing to correct a factual error; only the corrected text is used here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the official 20-page opinion’s opening and procedural history, its reproduction of the 1864 resolution and 1866 act, the background to the Tribe’s later claim, the statutory and Nonintercourse Act analysis, the court’s conclusion, and the rehearing correction (PDF pp. 1–5, 8–10, 12–17, 20). The underlying 1866 legislative record, district-court docket, original 1992–1994 correspondence, and later treatment of the ruling were not independently checked. Historical facts recounted by the opinion remain attributed to the court and cited sources.

Patrick Anthony DeRoche — In Pursuit of the Panzacola: A Historical Documentary and Archaeological Investigation ↗

DeRoche’s introduction explicitly places the historical Panzacola people around present-day Pensacola Bay in West Florida using seventeenth-century documentary accounts. His discussion distinguishes this people from the archaeological Pensacola culture; the test excavation did not establish a positive Panzacola site identification. Inspection: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review. Limits: The canonical name Pensacola is retained; Panzacola is the historical people-label used by the thesis. The later city and archaeological culture are separate referents. No definitive excavated Panzacola village, coordinates, ethnicity-from-ceramics inference, contemporary recognition status or disappearance claim is adopted. This is an original student thesis with committee oversight, not a statement of consensus on every historical identification.

Removal from Texas — Wichita History, August 2012 newsletter, pp. 2–3 ↗

Wichita and Affiliated Tribes. 2012. “Removal from Texas.” Wichita and Affiliated Tribes Newsletter, August, 2–3.

Publication: 2012-08

A substantial Tribal history article distinguishes Waco and Tawakoni removal from the Brazos Reserve from the Wichita and Keechi journey through the Fort Arbuckle area. It follows later displacement and village rebuilding. This is the publisher’s retrospective account, drawing on Earl H. Elam’s 2008 book; it is not a direct inspection of the removal reports.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete “Wichita History / Removal from Texas” article on printed pp. 2–3 (PDF pages 2–3; extracted lines 113–204), including all eleven endnotes. Issue cover inspected for August 2012 date and publisher. Adjacent employment notices, personal news, photographs and the rest of the issue were not reviewed for the proposal.

Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters ↗

Four linked chapters explain the Tribe’s historical account from early encounters through village life, displacement and continuing community. The credits identify a cooperative exhibit. Treat the chapters as one work, keep named historical groups distinct, and attribute archaeological, treaty and continuity interpretations rather than turning the narrative into independently checked archival evidence.

The Battle of Dove Creek ↗

Publication: 1950-04

Pool’s 19-page article reconstructs the January 8, 1865 Dove Creek battle using military correspondence and other records. This review inspected selected pages 367, 375, 379, and 385 only; the rest of the article was not read. The excerpt documents the attackers’ uncertain identification of the camp and the author’s reliance on conflicting reports. Its mid-20th-century military-history framing is attributed to Pool, and the article is not treated as a Kickapoo community account or as independent confirmation of every casualty or movement claim.
